content.title: Three trees
content.prompt: Explain the relationship between the widget tree, element tree and render tree in Flutter. Why does Flutter need all three?
guiding_questions: What is immutable and what is not?
What does the element do during rebuild?
Where does layout and painting happen?
content.model_answer_notes: A strong answer explains that widgets are cheap immutable configuration, elements are the persistent instances that hold state and position in the tree and diff new widgets against old ones, and render objects perform layout, painting and hit-testing. The separation lets Flutter rebuild widget descriptions constantly while reusing expensive render objects. Senior candidates mention keys, the `canUpdate` check (runtimeType and key), and why rebuilding a widget is not the same as re-laying-out its render object.

content.title: Choosing state management
content.prompt: A team is starting a mid-size Flutter app. How would you choose between Riverpod, Bloc and plain ChangeNotifier, and what would you actually recommend?
guiding_questions: What properties matter: testability, boilerplate, scoping?
What does the team already know?
content.model_answer_notes: Strong answers frame the choice around testability, how state is scoped and disposed, and team familiarity, rather than declaring a winner. They separate ephemeral UI state (setState is fine) from app state. They mention that Riverpod gives compile-safe providers without BuildContext, Bloc enforces event/state discipline useful for larger teams, and ChangeNotifier is adequate for small apps. The best answers add: keep business logic framework-agnostic so the choice is reversible.

content.title: Diagnosing jank
content.prompt: A screen in your Flutter app drops frames when scrolling. Walk me through how you diagnose and fix it.
guiding_questions: Which tool do you open first?
UI thread vs raster thread: how do you tell?
content.model_answer_notes: Expect DevTools performance overlay and timeline, distinguishing UI thread (build/layout) from raster thread (shader compilation, large images, opacity/clip layers). Common causes: rebuilding large subtrees because state is too high in the tree, expensive work in build, unconstrained ListView children without itemExtent, images not cached or resized, saveLayer from Opacity/ShaderMask. Fixes: const widgets, RepaintBoundary, splitting widgets, precaching, using ListView.builder, avoiding Opacity on animations (use AnimatedOpacity or FadeTransition). Senior answers mention impeller and shader warm-up history.

content.title: Platform channels
content.prompt: Explain how platform channels work and when you would use them versus FFI or an existing plugin.
content.model_answer_notes: MethodChannel sends asynchronous messages encoded with the StandardMessageCodec to platform code on the platform thread; results return as Futures. EventChannel streams events. Use channels for platform APIs (Bluetooth, sensors, native UI). Use dart:ffi for calling C libraries synchronously with lower overhead. Prefer pub.dev plugins when maintained. Mention error handling with PlatformException, the need to keep heavy work off the platform main thread, and Pigeon for type-safe generated channels.

content.title: Isolates vs async
content.prompt: What is the difference between async/await and isolates in Dart, and when do you need an isolate?
content.model_answer_notes: Dart is single-threaded per isolate with an event loop; async/await yields while waiting on I/O but CPU-bound work still blocks the UI. Isolates run on separate threads with separate heaps and communicate by message passing (copying, or transferring TypedData). Use compute or Isolate.run for parsing large JSON, image processing, crypto. Mention that isolate spawn has cost, and that since Dart 2.15 isolate groups make spawning and sending immutable objects cheaper.

content.title: Testing strategy
content.prompt: Describe your testing pyramid for a production Flutter app and what you would refuse to skip.
guiding_questions: Unit vs widget vs integration: what does each catch?
How do you test navigation and async state?
content.model_answer_notes: Most tests should be fast unit tests of business logic that does not depend on Flutter. Widget tests cover interaction and rendering with pumpWidget and fakes for dependencies. A small set of integration tests on real devices or emulators cover critical flows (login, payment). Golden tests catch visual regressions but need care across platforms. Non-negotiables: CI running tests on every PR, dependency injection to make logic testable, and testing error and loading states, not just happy paths.

content.title: Server vs client components
content.prompt: Explain React Server Components in Next.js. How do you decide what runs on the server and what runs on the client?
guiding_questions: What can a server component not do?
How do props cross the boundary?
content.model_answer_notes: Server components render on the server, can access data sources directly, and ship no JavaScript; client components ('use client') handle interactivity, state and browser APIs. Push the boundary as low as possible: interactive leaves are client, layouts and data fetching are server. Props across the boundary must be serializable. Mention streaming with Suspense, server actions for mutations, and the common mistake of marking whole pages as client because one button needs state.

content.title: Sessions vs JWTs
content.prompt: For a web app with a mobile client, would you use server sessions or JWTs? Defend your choice and explain the security tradeoffs.
content.model_answer_notes: Strong answers do not pick one blindly. Server sessions are simple to revoke and store nothing sensitive client-side, with cookies (httpOnly, Secure, SameSite) for browsers. JWTs suit stateless services and mobile clients but revocation requires short expiry plus refresh tokens or a denylist. Discuss storage: httpOnly cookies for web (CSRF considerations), secure storage on mobile. Mention algorithm pinning, key rotation and not putting sensitive data in JWT payloads. A common hybrid: opaque session tokens issued by an auth service, validated via introspection or a signed short-lived access token.

content.title: N+1 and query performance
content.prompt: An endpoint has become slow as data grew. Walk me through how you would find and fix the problem, including N+1 queries.
guiding_questions: How do you measure before guessing?
What is an N+1 and how do you detect it?
When is caching the wrong fix?
content.model_answer_notes: Measure first: request tracing, slow query log, EXPLAIN ANALYZE. N+1 shows as one query per row in a loop; fix with eager loading, joins or batched IN queries (DataLoader pattern in GraphQL). Check indexes on filter and join columns, avoid SELECT *, paginate with keyset instead of OFFSET for large tables. Caching hides the problem and adds invalidation complexity; use it after the query is sane. Senior candidates mention connection pooling limits and that ORMs make N+1 easy to introduce silently.

content.title: Cache invalidation strategy
content.prompt: Design the caching strategy for a product catalogue API with frequent price updates. Where do you cache and how do you invalidate?
guiding_questions: What are the layers: CDN, application, database?
content.model_answer_notes: Layers: CDN or edge cache for anonymous GETs with short TTL and stale-while-revalidate; application cache (Redis) keyed by product id with explicit invalidation on price change events; database query cache is rarely worth it. Use cache-aside for reads, publish invalidation on writes, and accept short staleness with a documented bound. Mention thundering herd protection (request coalescing, jittered TTLs), versioned keys, and that prices might need to be read-through at checkout regardless of cache.

content.title: Designing a REST API
content.prompt: What makes a REST API well designed? Give concrete rules you enforce and one you deliberately break.
content.model_answer_notes: Rules: nouns for resources, HTTP verbs for actions, consistent error envelope with machine-readable codes, cursor pagination, filtering via query params, idempotency keys for POSTs that create payments, explicit versioning strategy, OpenAPI as the contract, sensible status codes. Deliberately broken: strict HATEOAS almost nobody needs; RPC-style endpoints for actions that are not resources (POST /orders/{id}/cancel). Senior answers discuss backwards compatibility and rate limiting.

content.title: OWASP top risks
content.prompt: Name the web vulnerabilities you check for in every code review and explain how each is prevented in a Node or Laravel stack.
guiding_questions: Injection, XSS, CSRF, broken access control?
What does the framework handle and what does it not?
content.model_answer_notes: Injection: parameterized queries and ORMs. XSS: output encoding by default in templates, CSP, no dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data. CSRF: SameSite cookies and framework tokens. Broken access control: authorize on every request server-side, never trust client roles. Also: secrets in environment not code, dependency scanning, rate limiting on auth, secure headers, and logging without sensitive data. Strong answers note that frameworks handle the easy 80 percent and access control is where real breaches happen.

content.title: Improving RAG quality
content.prompt: Your RAG system gives confident wrong answers. What are the likely causes and how do you fix them systematically?
guiding_questions: Is it retrieval or generation failing?
How do you evaluate each stage?
content.model_answer_notes: Separate retrieval failure (right document not in top-k) from generation failure (right document present, wrong answer). Build an evaluation set with questions and gold passages; measure recall@k for retrieval and faithfulness for generation. Fixes for retrieval: better chunking (semantic, with overlap and metadata), hybrid search (BM25 plus embeddings), reranking, query rewriting. Fixes for generation: citations required, instruct to abstain when context is insufficient, smaller context with only top passages. Strong answers mention evaluation before changing anything.

content.title: Embeddings explained
content.prompt: Explain what embeddings are, how similarity search works, and one situation where embeddings fail badly.
content.model_answer_notes: Embeddings map text (or images) to dense vectors where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric closeness. Search uses approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF) with cosine or dot-product similarity. Failure modes: exact identifiers, product codes and negations, where lexical search wins; domain shift when the embedding model was not trained on the vocabulary; long documents averaged into a single vector. Mention dimensionality, normalization and that embedding model choice affects everything downstream.

content.title: When not to build an agent
content.prompt: When is an agentic architecture the wrong choice, and what would you build instead?
guiding_questions: What is the cost of autonomy?
How do you keep it observable?
content.model_answer_notes: Agents add latency, cost, non-determinism and debugging difficulty. If the task has a known sequence of steps, a workflow (deterministic orchestration with LLM calls at specific points) is cheaper and more reliable. Reserve agents for open-ended tasks where the path is unknown and tool use must be decided at runtime. Strong answers mention bounded loops, tool-call limits, human checkpoints, evaluation harnesses and tracing, and starting with the simplest thing that works.

content.title: Evaluating an LLM feature
content.prompt: How do you evaluate an LLM-powered feature before and after launch, without relying on vibes?
content.model_answer_notes: Offline: a curated test set with expected behaviours, rubric-based scoring, LLM-as-judge calibrated against human labels, and regression runs on every prompt or model change. Online: task completion, thumbs, edit distance on outputs, escalation rate, latency and cost per task. Mention that judge models share biases with the model under test, that small eval sets are noisy, and that logging real failures back into the eval set is the flywheel.

content.title: Latency and cost of inference
content.prompt: A feature calls an LLM on every keystroke and is too slow and expensive. What do you change?
content.model_answer_notes: Debounce and only call on pause; stream tokens to show progress; cache by normalized input; use a smaller or distilled model for the frequent path and a large model for the rare path; prompt caching for shared prefixes; shorten prompts; batch where possible. Set a cost budget per user action. Senior candidates question whether the LLM call belongs on every keystroke at all.

content.title: Overfitting in plain terms
content.prompt: Explain overfitting to a product manager and how you would detect it in a model you shipped.
content.model_answer_notes: Overfitting is memorizing the examples instead of learning the rule, like a student who memorizes past exam answers. Detect it by a gap between training and validation performance, and in production by drift when real data differs from training data. Mention holdout sets, cross-validation, regularization and monitoring. The best answers use one analogy and stop.

content.title: Design a URL shortener
content.prompt: Design a URL shortener that handles 100 million new links a month and 10 billion redirects. Talk through storage, ID generation and read path.
guiding_questions: Read/write ratio and what it implies?
How do you generate unique short IDs?
content.model_answer_notes: Read-heavy: cache aggressively (CDN and Redis) in front of a key-value store. IDs: base62 of a counter (needs coordination), or pre-generated key ranges per node, or hashing with collision check. Estimate storage (100M/month × ~500 bytes). Redirect path must be fast: cache hit, 301 vs 302 tradeoff for analytics. Mention rate limiting, abuse, expiry and analytics via async event stream. Strong candidates state assumptions and numbers before drawing boxes.

content.title: CAP in practice
content.prompt: Explain the CAP theorem and give one real system decision where you chose availability over consistency, or the reverse.
guiding_questions: Why is CA not a real choice?
content.model_answer_notes: During a network partition a distributed system must choose to stay available (serve possibly stale data) or consistent (refuse some requests). Partitions are inevitable, so the choice is AP or CP under partition; outside partitions the tradeoff is latency vs consistency (PACELC). Examples: shopping cart favours availability; payment ledger favours consistency. Strong answers avoid treating CAP as three equal knobs and mention tunable consistency in systems like Cassandra or DynamoDB.

content.title: Message queue guarantees
content.prompt: You are adding a queue between services. Explain at-least-once versus exactly-once delivery and how you make consumers safe.
content.model_answer_notes: At-least-once is the practical default: messages may be redelivered after failures, so consumers must be idempotent (dedupe by message id, upsert semantics, idempotency keys). Exactly-once end to end is only achievable with transactional outbox plus idempotent consumers, or within a single system like Kafka transactions. Discuss dead-letter queues, backoff, poison messages, ordering per key, and the outbox pattern to avoid dual writes.

content.title: Sharding a database
content.prompt: Your PostgreSQL primary is at capacity. Walk through the options before and including sharding.
content.model_answer_notes: Before sharding: query and index optimization, connection pooling (PgBouncer), read replicas, caching, archiving cold data, vertical scaling, table partitioning. Sharding: choose a key with even distribution and locality (tenant id), route in the application or via a proxy (Citus, Vitess-style), handle cross-shard queries and transactions by design, and plan resharding from day one. Strong answers stress that sharding is a last resort with permanent complexity.

content.title: Service boundaries
content.prompt: How do you decide where to draw service boundaries, and what is the most common mistake you have seen?
content.model_answer_notes: Boundaries follow business capabilities and team ownership, with each service owning its data. Signs of a bad boundary: chatty synchronous calls, shared databases, changes that always touch multiple services. Common mistake: splitting by technical layer or by entity (a 'user service' that everyone depends on). Mention starting with a modular monolith and extracting when a boundary proves stable.

content.title: Design a rate limiter
content.prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter for a public API. Which algorithm, where does state live, and how does it fail?
content.model_answer_notes: Token bucket or sliding window log/counter in Redis with atomic Lua scripts, keyed by API key or IP. Local approximate limits at each gateway node reduce latency, synced periodically. Return 429 with Retry-After headers. Decide fail-open (availability) vs fail-closed (protection) per endpoint. Mention clock skew, hot keys and distinguishing burst from sustained limits.

content.title: Selling a debt paydown
content.prompt: The board wants features. Engineering says the platform needs a quarter of cleanup. How do you decide, and how do you present it?
guiding_questions: How do you quantify the cost of the debt?
Is it really a full quarter?
content.model_answer_notes: Translate debt into business terms: lead time, incident cost, onboarding time, features blocked. Avoid all-or-nothing; propose a percentage allocation (e.g. 20–30 percent) tied to specific outcomes and measured monthly. Present options with risks, not an ultimatum. Show what happens if nothing is done. Strong answers acknowledge that some 'cleanup' is engineers' preference rather than business need, and that the CTO's job is to tell the difference.

content.title: First ten engineers
content.prompt: You are the first CTO. How do you hire the first ten engineers, and what would you do differently from a big-company process?
guiding_questions: What profile do you need at this stage?
How do you assess without a hiring machine?
How do you avoid cloning yourself?
content.model_answer_notes: Early hires need breadth, ownership and tolerance for ambiguity more than deep specialization. Use work-sample interviews close to real work, paid trial projects when possible, references done seriously, and sell the mission honestly. Hire for complementary strengths and set the bar on judgment and communication. Mention the risk of hiring only from your network, and setting culture through the first few hires.

content.title: Running a major incident
content.prompt: Describe how you run a severity-one incident from the first alert to the post-mortem, including what you personally do.
guiding_questions: How often do you update stakeholders?
What does a blameless post-mortem require?
content.model_answer_notes: Declare early, assign an incident commander (often not the CTO), a communications lead and a scribe; keep a single channel and timeline; update stakeholders at fixed intervals even when nothing changed; prioritize mitigation over root cause. The CTO shields the team from executives, makes trade-off calls (rollback, disable feature) and owns external communication. Post-mortem within days, blameless, with actions that have owners and dates. Mention that avoiding heroics and reducing time-to-detect are bigger levers than any single fix.

content.title: Cutting cloud spend
content.prompt: Cloud costs doubled year over year. Walk through how you approach it in the first thirty days.
guiding_questions: How do you keep it from creeping back?
content.model_answer_notes: First get attribution: tag resources by team and service, review the bill by line item. Quick wins: idle resources, over-provisioned instances, unattached storage, egress, logging retention, reserved or committed-use discounts. Structural: autoscaling, right-sizing databases, moving batch workloads. Give teams cost dashboards and budgets so spend becomes a visible engineering metric. Strong answers pair cost with reliability and do not cut redundancy blindly.

content.title: Explaining a migration to the CEO
content.prompt: You need to explain to a non-technical CEO why a six-month migration is necessary. Do it now, in two minutes.
guiding_questions: What is the business risk of not doing it?
What does the CEO need to decide?
content.model_answer_notes: Lead with the business outcome and the risk, not the technology. Give a plain analogy, a timeline with checkpoints, what the team will and will not deliver during the migration, and the decision you are asking for. Avoid jargon entirely. Strong answers include how progress will be reported and what would cause you to stop.

content.title: Data breach response
content.prompt: You learn a contractor's laptop with production credentials was stolen. What do you do in the first hour, first day and first week?
guiding_questions: How do you communicate internally and externally?
content.model_answer_notes: Hour one: rotate the credentials, revoke sessions and keys, preserve logs, open an incident with legal and security. Day one: determine what was accessed, scope the data, notify leadership, prepare regulator and customer notifications as required (GDPR 72 hours). Week one: forensic review, customer communication, root causes (why were long-lived credentials on a laptop), and control improvements such as short-lived credentials, device management and least privilege. Strong answers stay calm, sequence actions, and involve legal early.

content.title: Sixty-second pitch
content.prompt: Pitch a product you would build in sixty seconds: problem, who has it, why now, and what you need.
guiding_questions: What is the problem in one sentence?
content.model_answer_notes: Great pitches are concrete: a specific customer, a painful problem, a believable insight, early evidence and a clear ask. Cut technology details unless they are the insight. Practice cadence: problem, solution, why now, traction, ask.

content.title: Why won't a big company do this?
content.prompt: An investor asks: if this works, why won't Google or Microsoft just build it? Answer.
content.model_answer_notes: Honest answers: incumbents might, but they are slow, distracted, and their incentives protect existing revenue. Your advantage is focus, speed, a specific customer segment they ignore, and a moat that compounds with data, workflow lock-in or community. Avoid claiming they cannot. Strong founders name the incumbent's likely move and their counter.

content.title: Choosing a pricing model
content.prompt: How would you price a B2B developer tool: per seat, usage-based or flat? Reason through it out loud.
guiding_questions: What behaviour does each model encourage?
content.model_answer_notes: Anchor pricing to the value metric the customer already tracks. Per seat is predictable but discourages adoption; usage-based aligns with value but scares finance teams; flat tiers simplify buying. Hybrids (platform fee plus usage) are common. Discuss the buyer persona, procurement, expansion revenue, and testing price early rather than defaulting to free.

content.title: Customer discovery interview
content.prompt: Run a five-minute customer discovery conversation with me as an engineering manager. Avoid leading questions.
guiding_questions: How do you find the real pain?
content.model_answer_notes: Ask about specific past events ('tell me about the last time…'), quantify pain (time, money, frequency), find current workarounds, and avoid pitching or asking 'would you use…'. Listen more than talk. Strong answers reference The Mom Test principles and end by asking who else has this problem.

content.title: Firing a co-founder's friend
content.prompt: Your co-founder's close friend is an early engineer who is now underperforming. Talk through how you handle it.
guiding_questions: How do you align with your co-founder?
content.model_answer_notes: Separate facts from feelings: document expectations and gaps, give clear feedback with a time-boxed plan, and align with the co-founder privately on the standard before acting. Be humane and fast if the plan fails; a lingering situation damages the team more than the departure. Discuss severance, communication to the team and protecting the relationship with the co-founder by making it about the company.

content.title: Saying no to a big customer
content.prompt: Your largest prospect will sign if you build a custom feature that does not fit the roadmap. What do you do?
guiding_questions: Is it custom or a general need in disguise?
What does the revenue mean at this stage?
content.model_answer_notes: Dig into the underlying need; often a custom ask is a general need phrased specifically. If truly custom, weigh runway impact against distraction, and consider pricing it as services or a paid pilot with a deadline. Say no clearly when it would fork the product. Strong answers mention that early enterprise deals can define the company for good or ill.

content.title: Disagreeing with a decision
content.prompt: Tell me about a time you strongly disagreed with a technical decision made above you. What did you do?
guiding_questions: What was the decision and your objection?
What happened, and were you right?
content.model_answer_notes: Use STAR. Show that you disagreed with data and respect, escalated appropriately, and then committed once the decision stood. Strong answers include being wrong at least sometimes and what you learned about influence.

content.title: A failure you owned
content.prompt: Describe a project that failed because of a decision you made. What would you do differently?
guiding_questions: What changed in how you work?
content.model_answer_notes: Pick a real failure with real consequences, own it without blaming others, and show a concrete change in behaviour since. Avoid humble-brags disguised as failures.

content.title: Influencing without authority
content.prompt: Tell me about a time you changed how a team worked without being their manager.
guiding_questions: How do you know it stuck?
content.model_answer_notes: Show understanding of others' incentives, a small pilot with visible results, and patience. Evidence that the change persisted after you stopped pushing is what distinguishes strong answers.

content.title: Ambiguous project
content.prompt: Tell me about the most ambiguous project you have led and how you created clarity.
guiding_questions: What was unclear: goal, scope, ownership?
content.model_answer_notes: Strong answers show a bias to write things down, define what done means, find the real decision maker, and ship something small to reduce uncertainty. Mention how you kept stakeholders aligned as the picture changed.

content.title: Hard feedback you received
content.prompt: What is the hardest feedback you have received, and what did you do with it?
content.model_answer_notes: Be specific and vulnerable without drama. Show that you sought to understand, changed behaviour, and checked back with the person. Generic feedback like 'work on delegation' with no story is a weak answer.

content.title: Too much to do
content.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had far more work than capacity. How did you decide what not to do?
guiding_questions: What framework did you actually use?
What was dropped and what happened?
content.model_answer_notes: Show explicit prioritization tied to impact, proactive communication of what would not get done, and negotiation rather than silent heroics. Mention the outcome of what was dropped.

content.title: Database failing at peak
content.role: You are the CTO of a 40-person e-commerce company.
content.situation: It is the evening of your biggest sales day. The primary PostgreSQL database is at 100 percent CPU, checkout is timing out, and the CEO has just joined the incident call asking what is happening.
content.prompt: Explain your response to the CEO and the team in the first thirty minutes: what you do, what you decide, and what you say.
guiding_questions: What do you say to the CEO in the first sixty seconds?
Mitigation options in order of speed?
What do you protect and what do you sacrifice?

content.title: Investor challenges burn
content.role: You are the technical co-founder of a seed-stage startup.
content.situation: In a board meeting an investor says engineering costs are too high for the revenue and asks why you have eight engineers instead of four.
content.prompt: Respond to the investor. Defend or concede, with numbers and a plan.
guiding_questions: What does each engineer's work map to in the plan?
What would you cut if forced?
What do you need the board to understand?

content.title: Senior engineer resigns
content.role: You are the head of engineering.
content.situation: Your most senior backend engineer, who owns the payments system alone, tells you privately they have another offer and are leaning toward leaving in two weeks.
content.prompt: Have the conversation with them, then explain what you do in the following two weeks.
guiding_questions: What do you tell the team?

content.title: Vendor breach
content.role: You are the CTO of a B2B SaaS company.
content.situation: Your authentication vendor announces a breach. You do not yet know whether your customers' data was affected. Customers are already emailing.
content.prompt: Explain what you do in the first two hours and draft, out loud, the first message to customers.
guiding_questions: What can you say truthfully right now?
What do you commit to and by when?
Who needs to be involved internally?

content.title: CEO wants to rewrite
content.role: You are a newly hired CTO.
content.situation: The CEO wants to rewrite the entire product in a new stack because the previous team 'made a mess'. The current system serves paying customers and has no tests.
content.prompt: Give the CEO your recommendation and reasoning in a way they will accept.
guiding_questions: What do you need to learn before recommending?

content.title: Customer demo goes wrong
content.role: You are the founder demoing to a prospective enterprise customer.
content.situation: Halfway through the demo the app crashes in front of their CTO and procurement lead.
content.prompt: Recover the room. Say what you would say in the next two minutes.
guiding_questions: Do you acknowledge or move on?
How do you turn it into a credibility moment?
